actual.name: Production Outage — Post-Deployment Cascade Failure
actual.description: A deployment was pushed to production. Within roughly 90 minutes, degradation alerts began firing. The on-call team chose to investigate root cause rather than rolling back immediately. Degradation escalated into a full cascade failure after 2 AM, triggering a complete production outage.

~00:30–01:00 AM (error rate rising, latency elevated)
Investigation mode — root cause analysis pursued; rollback deferred
Not executed before 2 AM

Microservices with circuit breakers; cascade risk above error-rate threshold ~8%

outcomes.description: Full production outage — all or majority of users unable to use the service; incident bridge opened; multiple teams paged; extended recovery time required
Significant engineering hours consumed during the outage and post-mortem

counterfactuals.name: Rollback Initiated Before 2 AM (~01:45 AM)
counterfactuals.description: On-call engineer triggers rollback to the previously-stable version at 01:45 AM — approximately 15 minutes before the cascade failure threshold — without waiting for root cause identification. All other conditions remain identical: the bad deployment exists, the same alerts fire, the same architecture is in place.

counterfactuals.description: Team decides to roll back, but the decision comes at 02:15 AM — after the cascade failure has already begun propagating. Rollback is initiated but the cascade has already tripped circuit breakers and taken dependent services down.

differences.aspect: Rollback timing relative to cascade threshold
differences.actual: Rollback never initiated before cascade; failure cascaded freely
differences.counterfactual: cf1: Rollback at 01:45 AM (before threshold) — cascade never triggered; cf2: Rollback at 02:15 AM (after threshold) — cascade already in progress

differences.actual: Complete production outage — 100% of users blocked
differences.counterfactual: cf1: Degraded experience for ~25 minutes, no complete outage; cf2: Full outage still occurs but shorter duration

differences.actual: Full outage lasting 2–4 hours (including cascade recovery and dependent-service restart)
differences.counterfactual: cf1: ~25–30 minutes degradation; cf2: ~2 hours (outage shortened but not eliminated)

differences.actual: Required circuit breaker resets, dependent service restarts, and state reconciliation in addition to rollback
differences.counterfactual: cf1: Rollback alone sufficient — no cascade state to clean up; cf2: Still required circuit breaker resets

differences.actual: Team under mounting pressure with incomplete information; investigation without a time-box
differences.counterfactual: cf1: Pre-agreed policy removes the judgment call under pressure; decision is automatic after 15-minute window

insights: The cascade failure is the decisive branching point — before it triggers, a rollback resolves the incident cleanly; after it triggers, a rollback only reduces duration, not severity
The 2 AM threshold in the question corresponds closely to the cascade failure onset, which is why it is the right boundary: rolling back before 2 AM = before cascade; after = during cascade
A late rollback (cf2) still improves outcomes versus the actual scenario but by far less than an early rollback — this is a non-linear payoff curve with a cliff at cascade onset

The core decision failure was not a lack of information but a lack of a pre-committed policy: the team had degradation alerts and a known-bad deployment, which together are sufficient grounds for rollback without root cause identification

Rollback cost before cascade (~25 min degradation) is roughly 8–10× lower than the actual outage cost (2–4 hours full outage), making early rollback strongly net-positive even if the issue turned out to be transient
lessons: Adopt a default rollback policy: if a deployment is followed within 90 minutes by sustained degradation alerts and root cause is not identified within 15 minutes, initiate rollback — do not wait for root cause
Instrument and publish the cascade failure threshold (e.g., 'error rate > 8% for > 5 minutes trips circuit breakers') so engineers have a measurable countdown, not a judgment call
Treat pre-cascade rollback cost and post-cascade recovery cost as explicitly different quantities in incident runbooks — this comparison makes the early-rollback decision obviously correct in advance
Run quarterly rollback drills so that rollback time is well-understood and fast; slow rollback procedures raise the cost of early rollback and create rational bias toward investigation

Add an automated rollback trigger as a future-state goal: if error rate exceeds threshold within N minutes of a deployment, page on-call AND propose automated rollback requiring only a single approval

interventionPoint.description: Initiate rollback to the previously-stable version immediately upon confirming sustained degradation following the deployment — without waiting for root cause identification. The go/no-go criterion is simply: (1) deployment occurred in the last 90 minutes AND (2) degradation alerts are sustained for > 15 minutes AND (3) root cause is not yet identified.
interventionPoint.timing: 01:45 AM window (before 2 AM and before the cascade failure threshold); the outer boundary of the safe window closes at approximately 02:00 AM when cascade propagation begins

01:00–01:59 AM — On-call team investigates; no rollback decision; error rate continues climbing
~02:00 AM — Error rate crosses cascade threshold; circuit breakers begin opening
02:00–02:15 AM — Cascade propagates to dependent services; health checks fail
02:15+ AM — Full production outage; bridge call opened; all-hands recovery begins
05:30–06:00 AM — Services fully restored after manual circuit-breaker resets and state reconciliation
causalChains.branchingPoint: 01:45 AM — the last moment at which a rollback decision would have resolved the incident before cascade onset
causalChains.divergence: In the actual world, the team continued investigation past the cascade threshold. In cf1, a rollback at 01:45 AM removes the bad version before error rate reaches cascade threshold; circuit breakers never open; no cascade propagation occurs.
